summary.text: Seven-year-old male castrated Birman cat that was asymptomatic at presentation, with persistent ALT elevation and incidental increases in liver enzyme activity. Physical examination showed no significant findings, there were no current medications or other medical conditions, and abdominal ultrasound was unremarkable.

Liver biopsy was laparoscopic with a rounded or mottled appearance and histopathology showing reduced portal vein diameter, arteriolar and biliary hyperplasia, hepatocellular vacuolation, lobular atrophy, periportal fibrosis and increased collagen deposit, leading to a diagnosis of primary portal vein hypoplasia. Bile culture showed no growth and rhodanine staining showed none.

The cat received SAMe, SPC and ursodeoxycholic acid for 9 months. Liver enzymes improved after initiating therapy and continued to improve after discontinuation, with ALT improving most. At time of writing the cat had a good quality of life with no concurrent disease or ongoing treatments.

summary.text: Fourteen-year-old female spayed domestic shorthair cat with diabetes mellitus and hyperthyroidism, on glargine insulin and methimazole, presenting with increased, mild lethargy, tiredness and increased liver enzymes. Examination found a grade III/VI holosystolic murmur and abdominal ultrasound showed a mild extrahepatic bile duct dilation.

Laparoscopic liver biopsy showed reduced portal vein diameter, arteriolar and biliary hyperplasia, lobular atrophy and increased collagen deposit with copper 280 ppm and scattered periportal stain uptake, consistent with a diagnosis of primary portal vein hypoplasia. No histologic hepatic lipidosis was reported and bile culture showed no growth.

For possible hepatic encephalopathy the cat received lactulose for 1 month and metronidazole for 3 months. Liver enzymes improved mildly after lactulose with a rise in TBili, then further after metronidazole; ALT was 1040 U/l one year after biopsy. Medications were stopped and the owner questionnaire reported good quality of life.

summary.text: Fourteen-year-old male castrated domestic shorthair cat with hyperthyroidism treated with sodium iodide I-131 two months before biopsy. It was asymptomatic with a grade II/VI holosystolic murmur and normal liver enzyme activity, and was included because abdominal ultrasound showed hyperechoic hepatic parenchyma during a hyperthyroidism work-up.

Laparoscopic liver biopsy showed reduced portal vein diameter, arteriolar and biliary hyperplasia, hepatocellular vacuolation and periportal fibrosis, with copper 140 ppm, no rhodanine staining and bile culture growing Staphylococcus warneri, supporting a diagnosis of primary portal vein hypoplasia. Enrofloxacin was started based on culture and sensitivity.

Follow-up biochemistry after 2 weeks kept liver enzymes within the reference interval. The cat was euthanized because of pulmonary nodules and pleural effusion on thoracic ultrasound, with no additional diagnostics or necropsy, and survival from biopsy was 288 days.

summary.text: Eight-year-old male castrated domestic shorthair cat with hypertrophic obstructive myopathy on clopidogrel and atenolol, asymptomatic at presentation with incidental increases in liver enzymes on routine biochemistry. Examination noted weight loss and a historic grade III/VI systolic murmur, and abdominal ultrasound showed a mottled hepatic parenchyma.

Laparoscopic liver biopsy showed reduced portal vein diameter, arteriolar and biliary hyperplasia, hepatocellular vacuolation, lobular atrophy, periportal fibrosis and increased collagen deposit, with copper 623 ppm, periportal copper stain uptake and bile culture growing Staphylococcus pseudintermedius, giving a diagnosis of primary portal vein hypoplasia. Biopsy re-evaluation showed periportal hepatitis interpreted as reactive or non-specific.

Treatment included penicillamine for increased copper, which was inconsistently given and stopped because of gastrointestinal upset, one week of amoxicillin-clavulanic acid, and SAMe, SPC and ursodeoxycholic acid. article_limitations: Five-cat retrospective case series; patients are numbered by Table 1 row order because the abstract describes the cats only as a cohort and the first individual identity evidence is the Table 1 rows.

Cohort statements (3/5 cats asymptomatic, one cat well-controlled diabetic and hyperthyroid, 3/5 alive, one euthanized for unrelated causes, mean survival 878.5 days, enzyme means and ranges) are not copied to individual cats unless a labelled sentence supports them.
The results text gives the ALT range as 27–211 U/l whereas Table 2 lists 2111 for cat 2; recorded as an ambiguity, the table cell is kept as printed.

Table 2 bold cells are literal <bold> markup in the source XML, defined by the footnote as outside the reference interval. No flag is derived from the reference intervals.
